rationale: The iframe wraps a video player but carries no title attribute and no aria-label/aria-labelledby, so the frame is exposed with no accessible name. A keyboard or screen reader user cannot determine which frame to enter or what it contains.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The objective of this technique is to demonstrate the use of the title attribute of the iframe element to describe the contents of the frame... The title allows users to determine which frame to enter and explore."

rationale: title="" supplies an empty accessible name for a frame that embeds an interactive map, so the frame is effectively unnamed. An empty title fails the H64 requirement for a non-empty description of the frame contents.
citation: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): "For all user interface components ... the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies."

rationale: title="frame" is generic boilerplate that names the element type rather than the contact form inside, so it does not let a user identify or distinguish this frame from any other. A descriptive, content-specific title is required.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 frame condition: each frame must have a non-empty title/name that describes the content of the frame; a generic value such as "frame" does not describe the content.

rationale: title="iframe" describes the HTML element type and conveys nothing about the live-chat widget inside, so it does not help a user decide whether to enter the frame. The accessible name fails to identify the frame's purpose.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The title allows users to determine which frame to enter and explore." A title that merely repeats the element name does not meet this objective.

rationale: title="content" is uninformative: the frame holds a promotional advertisement, yet the name gives no clue about that, so the frame's purpose cannot be programmatically determined in any meaningful way.
citation: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): "For all user interface components ... the name and role can be programmatically determined ... including assistive technologies."

rationale: title="embedded content" is generic placeholder text that fails to describe the feature poll inside the frame, so an AT user cannot tell what this frame offers. H64 requires the title to describe the actual contents.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The objective of this technique is to demonstrate the use of the title attribute of the iframe element to describe the contents of the frame."

rationale: title="page" is a non-descriptive generic word that tells the user nothing about the June 2026 event calendar embedded in the frame, so it does not satisfy the programmatic-name requirement.
citation: EN 301 549 clause 9.4.1.2 (maps to WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value): the name of a user interface component, including a frame, must be programmatically determinable; "page" does not name the frame's content.

rationale: title="frame-1" is a machine-generated identifier, not a human-meaningful description of the payment form inside, so users cannot determine the frame's purpose from its name. An ID token does not describe content.
citation: Failure F65 analogue (missing programmatic name on the embedded component): an iframe whose only name is an opaque identifier provides no name that identifies its content, leaving the embedded payment component without a usable accessible name.

rationale: aria-label="" takes precedence over the title attribute in the accessible name computation, so despite title="Weather widget" the frame is exposed with an empty name. The override silences the only descriptive text.
citation: WAI-ARIA: an iframe is exposed as a frame and its accessible name should describe its purpose/content; an empty aria-label overrides the title and leaves the frame with no programmatically determinable name (SC 4.1.2).

rationale: The title contains only whitespace, which trims to an empty accessible name, so the comments-thread frame is effectively unnamed just like a missing title. A whitespace title does not describe the contents.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 frame condition: each frame must have a non-empty, descriptive title/name that describes its content; a whitespace-only title is treated as empty and non-descriptive.

rationale: title="Weather widget" actively misidentifies the frame, which actually contains an account login form, so the programmatic name describes the wrong content and misleads users about what they will encounter on entry.
citation: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): "the name and role can be programmatically determined ... including assistive technologies." A name that does not correspond to the component's content fails to programmatically determine the frame's true purpose.

rationale: title="Newsletter signup" does not match the video player inside the frame, so a screen reader user is told the frame is a form when it is media. The mismatched name fails to identify the actual content.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The objective ... is to ... describe the contents of the frame ... The title allows users to determine which frame to enter and explore." A title describing different content defeats that objective.

rationale: title="Product demo video: smart thermostat" is a non-empty, specific description that matches the video player and its subject inside the frame, so the frame's purpose is programmatically determinable and identifiable.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The objective ... is to ... describe the contents of the frame ... The title allows users to determine which frame to enter and explore."

rationale: title="Map of office location: 123 Main St" names the frame's purpose and the specific address rendered on the embedded map, so the accessible name accurately describes the content and users can decide whether to enter.
citation: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): "the name and role can be programmatically determined ... including assistive technologies." The title provides a programmatically determinable name matching the frame content.

rationale: title="Newsletter signup form" exactly describes the email subscription form embedded in the frame, so the accessible name correctly identifies the content and meets H64.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 frame condition: each frame must have a non-empty, descriptive title/name that describes its content; this title names the embedded signup form.

rationale: title="Customer support chat" matches the live-chat widget inside the frame, so the frame is given an accurate, non-generic accessible name that identifies its purpose to assistive technology.
citation: WAI-ARIA: an iframe is exposed as a frame and its accessible name should describe its purpose/content; "Customer support chat" describes the embedded chat content.

rationale: title="Payment checkout (Stripe)" names the embedded card-payment form and its provider, matching the content, so the frame's purpose is clearly and programmatically identifiable.
citation: EN 301 549 clause 9.4.1.2 (maps to WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value): the frame's name is programmatically determinable and accurately describes the embedded payment checkout.

rationale: aria-label="Quarterly sales dashboard" supplies an accurate accessible name that matches the metrics dashboard inside, so even without a title attribute the frame's purpose is programmatically determinable.
citation: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): "For all user interface components ... the name and role can be programmatically determined ... including assistive technologies." aria-label provides that name.

rationale: aria-labelledby references a visible heading reading "Event calendar - June 2026" that accurately names the calendar embedded in the frame, so the accessible name is descriptive and matches the content.
citation: WAI-ARIA: an iframe is exposed as a frame and its accessible name should describe its purpose/content; aria-labelledby points to a heading that names the frame's calendar content.

rationale: title="Cookie consent" matches the consent dialog embedded in the frame, so the accessible name correctly identifies the content and lets users decide whether to enter.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The title allows users to determine which frame to enter and explore."

rationale: title="Reader comments" accurately names the comments thread embedded in the frame, so the frame is given a content-specific accessible name that identifies its purpose.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 frame condition: each frame must have a non-empty, descriptive title/name that describes its content; "Reader comments" describes the embedded comments thread.

rationale: title="YouTube video: kayaking in Norway" names the platform and the specific subject of the embedded video player, matching the content, so the accessible name describes the frame accurately.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): "The objective ... is to ... describe the contents of the frame ... The title allows users to determine which frame to enter and explore."

rationale: title="Photo gallery" is non-empty and non-generic, so a deterministic title-presence detector sees a valid name and cannot confidently flag it; the failure is that the frame actually contains a customer-satisfaction survey, a mismatch that requires semantically reading the srcdoc. Hence abstain for the deterministic signal.
citation: Technique H64 (using the title attribute of the iframe element): the title must "describe the contents of the frame"; here the title names a gallery while the frame contains a survey, but confirming the mismatch requires reading the embedded content.

rationale: title="Interactive widget" is non-empty and not boilerplate like "frame"/"iframe", yet whether it is descriptive enough for the currency converter inside is a borderline judgment a title-presence detector cannot settle. Whether this is descriptive-enough or too-vague needs semantic reading, so the deterministic signal should abstain.
citation: SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A): "the name and role can be programmatically determined ... including assistive technologies." A name exists and is programmatically determinable; judging its descriptiveness against the content is beyond a presence-only deterministic check.
